abstract: Near-death experiences (NDEs) are a subset of non-ordinary states consciousness in which people frequently report unusual perceptions of space and self-motion. How the occurrence of self-motion varies across the visual-field boundary configurations described in first-person accounts remains underinvestigated. Alongside a semi-structured digital questionnaire, participants represented their NDE visual spaces schematically, outlining visual-field boundaries and marking self-location and self-motion direction. Across successive reconstructions, we examined visual-field geometry and extent in relation to self-location, the subjective experience of where one feels located, and self-motion, the perceived movement of the self through visual space. In spaces with reported self-motion, we also examined whether the movement was experienced as voluntarily initiated or controlled. Self-motion predominated in conical visual fields and in fields bounded by more strongly curved elliptic arcs. Self-motion was absent in most fields bounded by flatter elliptic arcs and in most fully ellipsoidal fields. Among spaces with self-motion, passive agency predominated in conical fields. Active agency was more frequent in ellipsoidal than in conical fields and was reported in half of the fully ellipsoidal fields with self-motion. Sparse data limited these exploratory comparisons. The analysis yielded no clear evidence of an association between perceived velocity magnitude and agency. These findings suggest that visual-field geometry is associated with whether self-motion occurs during the NDE Core and, when it occurs, with whether it is experienced as voluntarily initiated or controlled. The reconstruction approach provides a framework for investigating the spatial organization of first-person experience in NDEs.
